text: Production and testing both have a table called delivery_summary. A database scan and a scheduler describe that name. Is the matching table name enough to join their claims? Pause and explain what else you need.

Distinguish the environment, database and table. The catalogue uses prod/parcels/delivery_summary for production and a separate test identifier. Sources must agree which dataset they mean, recording a correspondence when names differ. A reused name may identify an unrelated replacement, so check identity before attaching old explanations.

Now assemble the page's invented catalogue entry. The database scan establishes that a percentage column exists. The scheduler reports which run published an output version. Service Analytics supplies the intended completed-delivery definition. These are separate claims about the same production dataset. An output version identifies one result; it does not replace the dataset identifier.

Look at the scan's times. It observed the column at nine in the morning; the catalogue received the record at two minutes past nine. When was the column created? Explain what those two times can establish before continuing.

Its creation time is unknown unless the source supplies that evidence. Nine is the observation time; two minutes past nine is collection time. For the scheduler record, completion occurred at five minutes past nine and collection followed a minute later. Arrival at the catalogue does not change when the source event occurred.

Keep each source attached to its claim. The scan cannot identify the run that wrote the values. The definition explains intended meaning, but does not prove the calculation follows it; inspect the run's inputs and code for that. The last record collected is not automatically an authority for every fact.

Keep responsibility explicit too. Service Analytics accepted responsibility in its definition record. Importing a team name alone does not establish that agreement or make the collector's operator responsible for the metric's meaning. Collecting descriptions brings evidence together; it does not settle every question.
